# Continuous integration and delivery {#sec-ch-ops-cicd}

> *"Continuous Integration is a software development practice where members

## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain **continuous integration**, **continuous delivery** and
  **continuous deployment** (and continuous training for ML), and the metrics
  used to judge a delivery process;
- design a pipeline as a DAG of stages, **prove** the order of sequential
  stages that minimises the expected cost (fail fast: by cost over failure
  probability) and compute the wall-clock time of parallel jobs (the critical
  path);
- write **GitHub Actions** workflows — triggers, jobs, steps, `needs`,
  matrices, caches, permissions, secrets — validate them with **actionlint**
  and run them locally with **act**;
- separate CI from CD, publish an image tagged by commit, and describe a
  deployment to Hugging Face Spaces;
- gate the promotion of a model with **McNemar's test** on paired
  predictions, proved from the binomial distribution.
:::

What CI/CD is and what it is for; the stages of a CI/CD pipeline; services
that run pipelines; GitHub Actions in practice; continuous delivery.

## CI/CD: what and why {#sec-ops-ci-what}

### Three practices, one pipeline

**Continuous integration** (CI) is the practice of merging every developer's
work into the shared main branch often — at least daily — with each merge
verified automatically by a build and the tests [@fowler2006]. Small, frequent
integrations keep conflicts small and make a failing test point at a small
change. **Continuous delivery** (CD) extends it: every change that passes the
pipeline produces an artefact that *could* be released, and releasing is a
button [@humble2010, ch. 1]. **Continuous deployment** goes one step further:
every passing change *is* released, automatically. ML adds **continuous
training** (CT): the pipeline that trains, validates and registers models runs
automatically on new data (@sec-ops-maturity).

Research on software delivery measures a team's process with four numbers —
**deployment frequency**, **lead time for changes** (commit to production),
**change failure rate** and **time to restore** service — and finds that
teams good at one tend to be good at all four: speed and stability are not
traded off but come together from small batches and automation
[@forsgren2018, ch. 2].

A pipeline is a set of **stages** with dependencies — a directed acyclic
graph. For the model service of this part:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-ops-pipeline
%%| fig-cap: "The pipeline of the sentiment service. CI (left) runs on every push and pull request; CD (right) runs on the main branch only, after CI succeeds. Stages in the same column can run in parallel."
flowchart LR
  subgraph CI["CI: every push / pull request"]
    F[format check] --> T[unit + contract tests]
    L[lint] --> T
    T --> B[build image]
    B --> S[smoke test the container]
  end

    G[model gate:<br/>challenger vs champion] --> P[push image<br/>tagged by commit]
    P --> D[deploy to staging,<br/>then production]

```

### The order of stages

Sequential stages stop at the first failure — there is no point building an
image whose tests fail. Each stage has a cost (minutes of runner time, or of
waiting) and a probability of failing. Which order minimises the expected
cost?

::: {#prp-ops-stage-order}
## Fail fast by cost over failure probability
Let stages $1, \dots, m$, independent, have costs $c_i > 0$ and failure
probabilities $p_i > 0$, and let a pipeline run them in an order $\pi$,
stopping at the first failure. Its expected cost is
$$
E[C_\pi] = \sum_{k=1}^{m} c_{\pi_k}\prod_{j<k}(1 - p_{\pi_j}),
$$ {#eq-ops-stage-cost}
and it is minimised by running the stages in increasing order of $c_i / p_i$
[@garey1973].
:::

*In one line:* run first what is cheap and likely to fail; an expensive check
that rarely fails goes last.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-stage-order
Stage $\pi_k$ runs if and only if all previous stages passed, which has
probability $\prod_{j<k}(1 - p_{\pi_j})$ by independence; linearity of
expectation gives @eq-ops-stage-cost. Consider two adjacent stages $i$ then
$j$ at positions $k, k+1$, and let $Q$ be the probability of reaching
position $k$. Their contribution is $Q(c_i + (1 - p_i)c_j)$; swapped,
$Q(c_j + (1 - p_j)c_i)$; the other terms do not change, since stages after
$k+1$ are reached with probability $Q(1 - p_i)(1 - p_j)$ in both orders. The
first order is no worse iff $c_i + c_j - p_ic_j \le c_j + c_i - p_jc_i$, i.e.
$c_i p_j \le c_j p_i$, i.e. $c_i/p_i \le c_j/p_j$. If an order is not sorted
by $c/p$, some adjacent pair is inverted and swapping it does not increase the
cost; repeating (bubble sort) reaches the sorted order without ever increasing
the cost, so the sorted order is optimal. $\blacksquare$
:::

Independent stages need not wait for each other: in a DAG, with enough
runners, a stage starts as soon as its predecessors finish.

::: {#prp-ops-critical-path}
## With parallel runners, time is the critical path
If every stage $v$ of an acyclic pipeline takes time $w_v$ and starts as soon
as all its predecessors have finished, and runners are unlimited, the pipeline
finishes at time
$$
T = \max_{\text{paths } P}\; \sum_{v \in P} w_v ,
$$ {#eq-ops-critical-path}
the weight of the heaviest (critical) path.
:::

*In one line:* each stage finishes at its own duration plus the latest finish
among its predecessors, so the finish times propagate along the longest
chain.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-critical-path
Let $f(v)$ be the finish time of $v$; then $f(v) = w_v + \max_{u \to v}
f(u)$ (with the maximum over an empty set equal to 0). By induction along a
topological order (@sec-ch-ops-orch proves one exists), $f(v)$ is the
heaviest weight of a path ending at $v$: true for sources, and if true for all
predecessors, the heaviest path to $v$ is $v$ appended to the heaviest path to
one of them. The pipeline ends at $\max_v f(v)$, the heaviest path overall.
$\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
stages = {  # name: (minutes, failure probability) — rough figures for the service's pipeline
    "format check": (0.2, 0.15), "lint": (0.3, 0.20), "tests": (2.0, 0.10),
    "build image": (4.0, 0.03), "smoke test": (1.0, 0.02),
}
def expected_cost(order):
    total, reach = 0.0, 1.0
    for s in order:
        c, p = stages[s]
        total += reach * c
        reach *= 1 - p
    return total

best = sorted(stages, key=lambda s: stages[s][0] / stages[s][1])
worst = max(itertools.permutations(stages), key=expected_cost)
print("c/p order :", " -> ".join(best), f"= {expected_cost(best):.2f} min")
print("worst     :", " -> ".join(worst), f"= {expected_cost(worst):.2f} min")
print("brute-force optimum:", f"{min(expected_cost(o) for o in itertools.permutations(stages)):.2f} min")
```

Real pipelines also have *precedence* (the smoke test needs the image), so
the ratio rule is applied among the stages that are free to move — here
format check, lint and tests — and the critical path decides how many of them
should run in parallel instead.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops6-ci-easy}
## Easy — two orders by hand
A pipeline has two independent checks: a lint that takes 0.5 minutes and
fails 20 % of the time, and a test suite that takes 6 minutes and fails 10 %
of the time. Compute the expected cost of both orders and check the $c/p$
rule. What if the tests failed 40 % of the time?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Lint first: $0.5 + 0.8 \cdot 6$. Tests first: $6 + 0.9 \cdot 0.5$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
for p_test in (0.10, 0.40):
    lint_first = 0.5 + (1 - 0.2) * 6
    tests_first = 6 + (1 - p_test) * 0.5
    print(f"tests fail {p_test:.0%}: lint first {lint_first:.2f} min, tests first {tests_first:.2f} min; "
          f"c/p lint {0.5 / 0.2:.1f}, tests {6 / p_test:.1f}")
```
Lint first costs 5.3 minutes on average against 6.45; the ratios agree (2.5
against 60). Even if the tests failed 40 % of the time, lint first would
still win (2.5 against 15): a cheap check should almost always come first.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-ci-medium}
## Medium — the rule against brute force
Generate 500 random pipelines of 6 independent stages (costs uniform in
$[0.1, 10]$, failure probabilities uniform in $[0.01, 0.5]$), and check that
the $c/p$ order always matches the brute-force optimum over the $6! = 720$
orders. Then measure how much worse, on average, the order "by cost only"
and "by failure probability only" are.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Compare expected costs, not orders: ties between equal ratios give several
optimal orders.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
def cost(order, c, p):
    total, reach = 0.0, 1.0
    for i in order:
        total += reach * c[i]
        reach *= 1 - p[i]
    return total

worse_c, worse_p, mismatches = [], [], 0
for _ in range(500):
    c, p = rng.uniform(0.1, 10, 6), rng.uniform(0.01, 0.5, 6)
    opt = min(cost(o, c, p) for o in itertools.permutations(range(6)))
    rule = cost(np.argsort(c / p), c, p)
    mismatches += not np.isclose(rule, opt)
    worse_c.append(cost(np.argsort(c), c, p) / opt - 1)
    worse_p.append(cost(np.argsort(-p), c, p) / opt - 1)
print(f"c/p rule not optimal in {mismatches} of 500 pipelines")
print(f"by cost only: +{np.mean(worse_c):.1%} on average; by failure probability only: +{np.mean(worse_p):.1%}")
```
The ratio rule matches the brute-force optimum every time, as
@prp-ops-stage-order proves. Ordering by cost alone is the better heuristic
of the two simple ones, but both lose several percent on average, and much more
on unlucky pipelines.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-ci-hard}
## Hard — critical path of a real workflow
A workflow has these jobs and durations (minutes): `format` 0.3, `lint` 0.5,
`unit` 3 (needs format, lint), `contract` 2 (needs format, lint), `build` 5
(needs unit, contract), `scan` 2 (needs build), `smoke` 1.5 (needs build),
`push` 1 (needs scan, smoke). Compute the wall-clock time with unlimited
runners and the critical path, and the time with a single runner. Which job
would you speed up first, and by how much can the total shrink if that job
became instantaneous?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Process the jobs in an order where every job comes after its `needs`, and
keep, for each job, its finish time and the predecessor that determined it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
jobs = {"format": (0.3, []), "lint": (0.5, []), "unit": (3, ["format", "lint"]),
        "contract": (2, ["format", "lint"]), "build": (5, ["unit", "contract"]),
        "scan": (2, ["build"]), "smoke": (1.5, ["build"]), "push": (1, ["scan", "smoke"])}

def critical_path(jobs):
    finish, prev = {}, {}
    for name in jobs:                       # the dict is already in a topological order
        w, needs = jobs[name]
        start = max((finish[n] for n in needs), default=0.0)
        prev[name] = max(needs, key=finish.get) if needs else None
        finish[name] = start + w
    end = max(finish, key=finish.get)
    path = [end]
    while prev[path[-1]]:
        path.append(prev[path[-1]])
    return finish[end], path[::-1]

T, path = critical_path(jobs)
print(f"unlimited runners: {T} min along {' -> '.join(path)}; one runner: {sum(w for w, _ in jobs.values())} min")
for j in path:
    faster = {k: ((0.0 if k == j else w), n) for k, (w, n) in jobs.items()}
    print(f"  if {j:6s} took 0 min: {critical_path(faster)[0]} min")
```
The critical path is lint → unit → build → scan → push, 11.5 minutes against
15.3 on one runner. Only jobs on the critical path matter: making `build`
instantaneous saves its full 5 minutes, making `unit` instantaneous saves only
1 minute, because `contract` then becomes the bottleneck — the critical path
moves. Speeding up `smoke` or `contract` alone saves nothing.
:::

## GitHub Actions {#sec-ops-gha}

### Workflows, jobs, steps

**GitHub Actions** runs pipelines defined as YAML **workflows** in
`.github/workflows/` [@githubactions2026]. A workflow has **triggers**
(`on:` — `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` with a cron expression,
`workflow_dispatch` for a manual button) and **jobs**; each job runs on a
fresh **runner** (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, a virtual machine) as a sequence
of **steps**, each either a shell command (`run:`) or a reusable **action**
(`uses: owner/repo@version`). Jobs run in parallel unless `needs:` orders them
— the DAG of @fig-ops-pipeline. Other essentials:

- **`strategy.matrix`** runs a job once per combination of values (Python
  versions, operating systems);
- **caches** (`actions/cache`, or the built-in cache of `setup-python`) save
  directories between runs under a key — typically a hash of the lock file,
  so the cache is invalidated exactly when dependencies change (the same
  content-addressing idea as image layers);
- **`permissions:`** sets what the job's automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN` may do
  (least privilege: `contents: read` unless more is needed);
- **secrets** (`${{ secrets.NAME }}`) are encrypted values set in the
  repository's settings, masked in logs and not available to workflows
  triggered from forks;
- **environments** group secrets and protection rules (required reviewers,
  allowed branches) for deployments.

This book is itself published by such a workflow: on every push to `main`, a
job renders the book and a second job, which `needs` the first, deploys it to
GitHub Pages (the repository's `.github/workflows/publish.yml`).

### A CI workflow for the service

The service, its tests and its Dockerfile from the previous chapters, in a
repository with this workflow:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
train = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=1)
model = ob.train_model(train.text, train.label)
repo = ob.make_service(ob.project("sentiment-repo"), model)
dev_pins = ["fastapi", "uvicorn", "pydantic", "scikit-learn", "numpy", "scipy", "joblib", "threadpoolctl"]
ob.write("requirements.txt", "\n".join(f"{p}=={version(p)}" for p in dev_pins), base=repo)
ob.write("requirements-dev.txt", "-r requirements.txt\n" + "\n".join(
    f"{p}=={version(p)}" for p in ["pytest", "pytest-cov", "httpx", "ruff"]), base=repo)
ob.write("pyproject.toml", """
    [tool.ruff]
    line-length = 100
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    select = ["E", "F", "W", "I", "B", "UP"]
    [tool.pytest.ini_options]
    pythonpath = ["."]
    addopts = "-q -p no:cacheprovider"
""", base=repo)
ob.write("tests/test_api.py", '''
    import os
    from pathlib import Path

    import pytest
    from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

    os.environ["MODEL_PATH"] = str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "model.joblib")


    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
    def client():
        from app import app

        with TestClient(app) as c:
            yield c


    def test_ready(client):
        assert client.get("/ready").status_code == 200


    @pytest.mark.parametrize("body", [{"texts": []}, {"texts": [""]}, {"texts": ["x" * 281]}])
    def test_rejects(client, body):
        assert client.post("/v1/predict", json=body).status_code == 422


    def test_clear_cases(client):
        r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"texts": ["love the new phone", "the battery is awful"]})
        assert [p["label"] for p in r.json()["predictions"]] == ["positive", "negative"]
''', base=repo)
ob.write("Dockerfile", """
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE}
    ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
    RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 app
    COPY app.py model.joblib ./
    ENV MODEL_PATH=/app/model.joblib
    USER app
    HEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --timeout=3s --start-period=5s --retries=3 \\
      CMD ["python", "-c", "import urllib.request as u; u.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/ready', timeout=2)"]
    CMD ["uvicorn", "app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
""", base=repo)
ob.run("python -m ruff format -q .", cwd=repo)
ob.write(".github/workflows/ci.yml", """
    name: CI

    on:
      push:
        branches: [main]
      pull_request:

    permissions:
      contents: read

    concurrency:                        # a newer push cancels the older run of the same branch
      group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
      cancel-in-progress: true

    jobs:
      quality:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        strategy:
          matrix:
            python-version: ["3.12", "3.13"]
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v7
          - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
            if: ${{ !env.ACT }}           # act runs on the local machine's Python
            with:
              python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
              cache: pip
              cache-dependency-path: requirements-dev.txt
          - name: Install dependencies
            run: python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
          - name: Format check
            run: python -m ruff format --check .
          - name: Lint
            run: python -m ruff check .
          - name: Tests
            run: python -m pytest

      image:
        needs: quality                  # only if every quality job passed
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v7
          - name: Build
            run: docker build --build-arg BASE=${{ vars.BASE_IMAGE || 'python:3.12-slim' }} -t sentiment:${{ github.sha }} .
          - name: Smoke test
            run: |
              docker run -d --name smoke -p 8000:8000 sentiment:${{ github.sha }}
              for i in $(seq 60); do curl -fs localhost:8000/ready && break; sleep 1; done
              curl -fs -X POST localhost:8000/v1/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\
                   -d '{"texts": ["love the new phone"]}' | grep -q '"label":"positive"'
          - name: Clean up
            if: always()
            run: docker rm -f smoke
""", base=repo)
ob.show(".github/workflows/ci.yml", base=repo)
```

Each part implements something from this part: the `quality` job runs the
checks of @exr-ops4-lint-hard, in the fail-fast order, on two Python
versions; the cache key is derived from the lock file; the `image` job builds
the image of @sec-ops-image and runs a **smoke test of meaning**
(@exr-ops5-what-hard) against the running container; `permissions` grants
read access only; `concurrency` cancels superseded runs.

### Checking and running a workflow locally

A typo in a workflow is found only when it runs — after a push. Two tools
shorten that loop. **actionlint** checks workflows statically: YAML
structure, expression syntax, the types of contexts (`github.sha`,
`matrix.*`), the inputs of known actions, and the shell scripts with
ShellCheck when available [@actionlint2026]. A workflow with three typical
mistakes:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
broken_dir = ob.project("broken-wf")
ob.write(".github/workflows/broken.yml", """
    name: broken
    on: push
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
            with:
              python_version: "3.13"
          - run: echo "testing ${{ github.shaa }}"
      deploy:
        needs: tests
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo deploying
""", base=broken_dir)
ob.show(".github/workflows/broken.yml", base=broken_dir)
ob.sh(f"{ob.tool('actionlint')} -no-color -oneline", cwd=broken_dir, shown="actionlint")
ob.sh(f"{ob.tool('actionlint')} -no-color", cwd=repo, shown="actionlint   # on the service's workflow")
```

actionlint caught an unknown input name (`python_version`), a property that
does not exist (`github.shaa`) and a dependency on a job that does not exist
(`tests`); the service's workflow passes.

**act** runs workflows locally, reading the same YAML [@act2026]. With
`-P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted` it runs the jobs directly on the local machine
instead of in a runner image (the build machine cannot download runner
images); actions are cloned from GitHub — here, from a local clone of each
action's repository, passed with `--local-repository`. act sets the
environment variable `ACT`, which the workflow uses to skip `setup-python`
locally. The repository is committed first, since `push` events refer to a
commit:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ob.write(".gitignore", "__pycache__/\n.coverage\n", base=repo)
ob.run("git init -q -b main && git add -A && git commit -qm 'Service, tests, Dockerfile and CI workflow'",
       cwd=repo, env=GITENV, check=True)
actions_dir = ob.WORK / "actions"
for action, ref in (("actions/setup-python", "v7"), ("actions/cache", "v6")):
    target = actions_dir / action.replace("/", "_")
    if not target.exists():
        ob.run(f"git clone -q --depth 1 -b {ref} https://github.com/{action} {target}", check=True)
cb.ensure_base_images()

def act(cwd, *extra, event="push"):
    cmd = (f"{ob.tool('act')} {event} -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted --no-cache-server "
           f"--local-repository actions/setup-python@v7={actions_dir / 'actions_setup-python'} "
           f"--local-repository actions/cache@v6={actions_dir / 'actions_cache'} "
           f"--var BASE_IMAGE={cb.LOCAL['python']} " + " ".join(extra))
    return cmd

def act_summary(text):
    keep = []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if re.search(r"⭐ Run Main|✅  Success - Main|❌  Failure - Main|🏁|\| (\d+ passed|\d+ failed|All checks|.*would be reformatted|TOTAL)", line):
            keep.append(re.sub(r" \[[\d.]+[µm]?s\]", "", line))
    return "\n".join(keep)

ob.sh(act(repo), cwd=repo, shown="act push -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted --var BASE_IMAGE=local/python:3.12-slim",
      filt=act_summary, timeout=1800, max_lines=80)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ACT_OK = ob.LAST.returncode == 0
```

Both matrix entries of `quality` ran the format check, lint and tests, and
`image` started only after both had succeeded, built the image and passed the
smoke test`{python} "" if ACT_OK else " (see the output: the run failed)"`. On
GitHub the same file runs on fresh virtual machines; the matrix entries then
really use Python 3.12 and 3.13, whereas locally both used the build
machine's Python.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops6-gha-easy}
## Easy — read a workflow
For the service's `ci.yml`: (a) how many jobs run for a push to a feature
branch with an open pull request, and for a push to `main`? (b) Which jobs
run in parallel? (c) What happens to the `image` job if the Python 3.12 tests
fail but the 3.13 ones pass? (d) What can a step of this workflow do with the
repository through `GITHUB_TOKEN`? (e) When is the pip cache invalidated?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
A matrix job counts once per combination; `needs` waits for *all* of them.
Look at the `on:` filters and at the `permissions:` block.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) A push to a feature branch does not match `push: branches: [main]`, but
the pull request's update triggers `pull_request`: two `quality` jobs (the
matrix) and, if they pass, `image` — three jobs. A push to `main` triggers the
same three. (b) The two matrix entries of `quality` run in parallel; `image`
waits. (c) `image` is skipped: `needs` requires every matrix job to succeed
(unless `fail-fast` and `if:` conditions say otherwise; by default the other
matrix job is also cancelled). (d) Only read the repository's contents
(`contents: read`): it cannot push, comment or publish packages. (e) When
`requirements-dev.txt` changes, since the cache key includes its hash.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-gha-medium}
## Medium — break it and watch it fail
Introduce, in turn, (a) an unformatted line, (b) an unused import, (c) a
failing test, into the service repository, commit each, and run the workflow
with act. Report which step fails and whether the `image` job runs. Then
restore the repository.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Run only the `quality` job (`act push -j quality`) to save time, and look at
the first failing step in act's output.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def break_and_run(edit, message):
    original = (repo / "app.py").read_text()
    edit()
    ob.run(f"git commit -qam '{message}'", cwd=repo, env=GITENV)
    p = ob.run(act(repo), cwd=repo, timeout=1800)
    out = p.stdout + p.stderr
    failed = sorted(set(re.findall(r"❌  Failure - Main ([^\[\n]+)", out)))
    ran_image = "[CI/image" in out
    ob.run("git reset -q --hard HEAD~1", cwd=repo)
    (repo / "app.py").write_text(original)
    return failed, ran_image

edits = {
    "unformatted": lambda: (repo / "app.py").write_text((repo / "app.py").read_text() + "\nx = [1,2]\n"),
    "unused import": lambda: (repo / "app.py").write_text((repo / "app.py").read_text().replace("import os\n", "import os\nimport sys\n")),
    "failing test": lambda: (repo / "tests" / "test_api.py").write_text(
        (repo / "tests" / "test_api.py").read_text().replace('== ["positive", "negative"]', '== ["negative", "positive"]')),
}
for name, edit in edits.items():
    failed, ran_image = break_and_run(edit, name)
    print(f"{name:14s} failing steps: {', '.join(s.strip() for s in failed) or 'none'}; image job ran: {ran_image}")
_ = ob.run("git checkout -q -- .", cwd=repo)
```
Each defect stops `quality` at its own step — format check, lint, tests — and
`image` never runs, so no image is built from a commit that fails its checks.
The order of the steps is the fail-fast order of @prp-ops-stage-order. A
common anti-pattern is `continue-on-error: true` on the lint step "to see all
problems at once", which then lets unlinted code through.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-gha-hard}
## Hard — a scheduled job and a cache key
Add to the workflow a second trigger, `schedule` (every night at 02:17 UTC),
under which a job `nightly` runs an extended test suite (marked `slow`) that
does not run on pushes. Use a cache for a downloaded evaluation file, keyed by
its expected SHA-256, so the file is downloaded only when the expected hash
changes. Validate with actionlint and run the `nightly` job locally with act
(the `schedule` event).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`if: github.event_name == 'schedule'` selects jobs by trigger; `pytest -m
slow` and `-m "not slow"` split the suite. Pick an odd minute for the cron
(many workflows run at :00, which delays them). The cache key can be any
string — put the hash in it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
wf = (repo / ".github/workflows/ci.yml").read_text()
wf = wf.replace("  pull_request:\n", "  pull_request:\n  schedule:\n    - cron: \"17 2 * * *\"     # every night, 02:17 UTC\n")
wf = wf.replace("            run: python -m pytest\n", "            run: python -m pytest -m \"not slow\"\n")
wf = wf.replace("  quality:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest", "  quality:\n    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest")
wf += """
  nightly:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      EVAL_SHA256: 3f0c5e4f0d1c2b3a4f5e6d7c8b9a0f1e2d3c4b5a69788796a5b4c3d2e1f0a9b8
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/cache@v6
        if: ${{ !env.ACT }}
        with:
          path: data/eval.csv
          key: eval-${{ env.EVAL_SHA256 }}
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - name: Extended tests
        run: python -m pytest -m slow
"""
(repo / ".github/workflows/ci.yml").write_text(wf)
ob.write("tests/test_slow.py", '''
    import sys

    import pytest


    @pytest.mark.slow
    def test_many_posts(client):
        texts = ["the camera is brilliant"] * 64
        for _ in range(20):
            r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"texts": texts})
            assert {p["label"] for p in r.json()["predictions"]} == {"positive"}
''', base=repo)
(repo / "tests/conftest.py").write_text("")
(repo / "pyproject.toml").write_text((repo / "pyproject.toml").read_text().replace(
    'addopts = "-q -p no:cacheprovider"', 'addopts = "-q -p no:cacheprovider"\nmarkers = ["slow: extended tests run nightly"]'))
(repo / "tests/test_slow.py").write_text((repo / "tests/test_slow.py").read_text().replace("import sys\n\n", ""))
# the session fixture lives in test_api.py: move it to conftest.py so both modules can use it
api = (repo / "tests/test_api.py").read_text()
fixture = api[api.index("import os"):api.index("def test_ready")]
(repo / "tests/conftest.py").write_text(fixture)
(repo / "tests/test_api.py").write_text("import pytest\n\n\n" + api[api.index("def test_ready"):])
ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format -q . && {PY} -m ruff check -q --fix .", cwd=repo)
ob.run("git add -A && git commit -qm 'Nightly extended tests'", cwd=repo, env=GITENV, check=True)
ob.sh(f"{ob.tool('actionlint')} -no-color && echo 'actionlint: no problems'", cwd=repo, shown="actionlint")
ob.sh(act(repo, event="schedule"), cwd=repo, shown="act schedule -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted",
      filt=act_summary, timeout=1800)
```
Under `schedule`, only `nightly` runs (the other jobs are skipped by their
`if:`), and it runs only the slow tests; on pushes the `-m "not slow"` filter
keeps them out of the fast loop. The cache key contains the expected hash of
the evaluation file, so changing the file means changing the hash in the
workflow, which changes the key — a cache can never serve a stale file under a
new name. (The hash in the workflow is a placeholder: in a real pipeline the
download step must also *verify* it, @exr-ops1-stack-hard.) Moving the
session fixture into `conftest.py` was needed for two test modules to share
it.
:::

## Continuous delivery and promotion gates {#sec-ops-cd}

### Separate CI from CD

CD runs only for commits that passed CI, usually only on the main branch,
and needs credentials that CI must not have. GitHub Actions expresses this
with a separate job (or workflow) that `needs` the CI jobs, runs `if:
github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, requests `packages: write` only for itself,
and reads its credentials from secrets or from an **environment** with
protection rules:

```yaml
  publish:
    needs: image
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write                    # push to the GitHub Container Registry
    environment: production              # protection rules, environment secrets
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/sentiment:${{ github.sha }}
```

The image is tagged with the **commit id**: every image can be traced to the
exact code that built it (@prp-ops-commit), and a deployment refers to it by
digest (@exr-ops5-rollback-digest).

**Hugging Face Spaces** can host a containerised demo: a Space of type Docker
is a Git repository whose `README.md` starts with a YAML header such as
`sdk: docker` and `app_port: 8000`; the platform builds the Dockerfile at the
root and runs it [@huggingface2026hub]. A CD job deploys by pushing the
repository's files to the Space's Git remote, authenticated by a token stored
as a repository secret (`HF_TOKEN`), e.g. `git push
https://user:$HF_TOKEN@huggingface.co/spaces/user/sentiment main`. The build
machine of this book cannot reach Hugging Face, so this step is described, not
run.

### A statistical gate for models

Before a retrained model (the **challenger**) replaces the one in production
(the **champion**), the pipeline should check that it is not worse. Both
models are evaluated on the **same** examples, so the comparison is *paired*:
only the examples on which they disagree carry information.

::: {#prp-ops-mcnemar}
## McNemar's exact test
On $n$ examples, let $b$ be the number the challenger gets right and the
champion wrong, and $c$ the number the champion gets right and the challenger
wrong. If the two models have the same accuracy on the population — more
precisely, if each discordant example is equally likely to be of either kind
— then, conditionally on $d = b + c$,
$$
c \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(d, \tfrac12),
$$
so the one-sided p-value for "the challenger is worse" is $P(X \ge c)$ with
$X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(d, \frac12)$ [@mcnemar1947].
:::

*In one line:* examples on which both models agree say nothing about which is
better; among the disagreements, a fair coin decides who wins if they are
equally good.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-mcnemar
Each example independently falls in one of four cells (both right, both
wrong, only challenger right, only champion right) with probabilities
$\pi_{11}, \pi_{00}, \pi_{10}, \pi_{01}$. The accuracies are $\pi_{11} +
\pi_{10}$ and $\pi_{11} + \pi_{01}$; they are equal iff $\pi_{10} = \pi_{01}$.
Given that an example is discordant, it is of the "champion right" kind with
probability $\pi_{01}/(\pi_{10} + \pi_{01}) = \frac12$ under equality. The
$d$ discordant examples are independent, so the number $c$ of the second kind
is $\mathrm{Binomial}(d, \frac12)$ conditionally on $d$. The p-value of the
observed $c$ for the alternative "champion better" is the probability of a
value at least as large under the null. $\blacksquare$
:::

The test uses $d$, not $n$: two models that agree on 95 % of the examples
are compared on the remaining 5 %, which is why a paired comparison detects
small differences with far fewer examples than comparing two independently
estimated accuracies (@exr-ops6-cd-medium).

```{python}
def mcnemar_worse(y, p_champion, p_challenger):
    """b, c and the one-sided exact p-value for 'the challenger is worse'."""
    right_ch, right_new = p_champion == y, p_challenger == y
    b = int(np.sum(right_new & ~right_ch))     # challenger right, champion wrong
    c = int(np.sum(right_ch & ~right_new))     # champion right, challenger wrong
    p = binom.sf(c - 1, b + c, 0.5) if b + c else 1.0
    return b, c, float(p)

evaluation = ob.make_posts(4000, seed=300)
y_ev = evaluation.label.to_numpy()
champion = model
candidates = {
    "retrained on a new sample": ob.train_model(ob.make_posts(3000, seed=5).text, ob.make_posts(3000, seed=5).label),
    "unigrams only": ob.train_model(train.text, train.label, ngram=(1, 1)),
}
p_champ = champion.predict(evaluation.text)
for name, ch in candidates.items():
    p_new = ch.predict(evaluation.text)
    b, c, p = mcnemar_worse(y_ev, p_champ, p_new)
    print(f"{name:26s} acc {np.mean(p_new == y_ev):.4f} vs {np.mean(p_champ == y_ev):.4f}; "
          f"b = {b:3d}, c = {c:3d}, p(worse) = {p:.2g} -> {'BLOCK' if p < 0.05 else 'pass'}")
```

The retrained model differs from the champion on about ninety posts, with
no significant difference — it may be promoted (if, say, it was trained on newer
data). The unigram model loses many more disagreements than it wins, and the
gate blocks it.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops6-cd-easy}
## Easy — McNemar by hand
On 1 000 posts, a challenger and a champion agree on 960. Of the 40
disagreements, the challenger is right on 14 and the champion on 26. Compute
the one-sided p-value for "the challenger is worse" with the binomial
distribution (and its normal approximation $z = (c - b)/\sqrt{b + c}$). Would
a gate at 5 % block the challenger? What do the 960 agreements contribute?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$c = 26$, $d = 40$: $P(X \ge 26)$ for $X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(40, 0.5)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
b_, c_ = 14, 26
print(f"exact p = {binom.sf(c_ - 1, b_ + c_, 0.5):.4f}; normal z = {(c_ - b_) / np.sqrt(b_ + c_):.2f}, "
      f"p = {norm.sf((c_ - b_) / np.sqrt(b_ + c_)):.4f}")
```
The exact p-value is about 0.04: a gate at 5 % blocks the challenger,
although its accuracy (0.948 against 0.960) differs by 1.2 points only. The
960 agreements contribute nothing to the test — they would be the same
whichever model is better.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-cd-medium}
## Medium — paired versus unpaired
A challenger is truly 1 point worse than the champion. By simulation (on the
synthetic posts, or with binomial draws), compare how often a 5 % gate catches
it with (a) McNemar's test on a shared evaluation set of $n$ posts and (b) a
two-proportion test on two separate evaluation sets of $n$ posts each, for $n
\in \{500, 2000, 8000\}$. Explain the difference.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Model the pair of outcomes per example: with probability $\pi_{11}$ both
right, $\pi_{10}$ only the champion, $\pi_{01}$ only the challenger,
$\pi_{00}$ neither, chosen so that the accuracies are 0.93 and 0.92 and the
models disagree on, say, 5 % of the examples.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
acc_old, acc_new, disagree = 0.93, 0.92, 0.05
pi10 = (disagree + (acc_old - acc_new)) / 2          # champion right only
pi01 = disagree - pi10                               # challenger right only
pi11 = acc_old - pi10
probs = [pi11, pi10, pi01, 1 - pi11 - pi10 - pi01]
for n in (500, 2000, 8000):
    caught_paired = caught_unpaired = 0
    for _ in range(2000):
        cells = rng.multinomial(n, probs)
        b, c = cells[2], cells[1]
        caught_paired += (b + c) > 0 and binom.sf(c - 1, b + c, 0.5) < 0.05
        k_old, k_new = rng.binomial(n, acc_old), rng.binomial(n, acc_new)
        pool = (k_old + k_new) / (2 * n)
        z = (k_old - k_new) / n / np.sqrt(2 * pool * (1 - pool) / n)
        caught_unpaired += norm.sf(z) < 0.05
    print(f"n = {n:5d}: paired (McNemar) {caught_paired / 2000:.2f}, unpaired {caught_unpaired / 2000:.2f}")
```
The paired test has much higher power at every size: the unpaired comparison
must see a 1-point difference through the full binomial noise of two
accuracies near 0.93 (variance $\approx 2 \cdot 0.93 \cdot 0.07/n$), while
McNemar looks only at the 5 % of examples where the models differ, where the
1-point gap is a 30/70 split. Evaluating both models on the same examples is
free — and the right design for a gate.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-cd-hard}
## Hard — the gate in the pipeline
Add to the service repository a script `gate.py` that loads the champion
(`model.joblib`) and a challenger (`challenger.joblib`), evaluates both on a
fixed evaluation set, prints a report and exits with status 1 when McNemar's
test says the challenger is worse at the 5 % level, 0 otherwise. Add a job
`gate` to the workflow that runs it, and a job `publish` that `needs` it.
Run the workflow with act twice: once with a challenger retrained on a new
sample, once with the unigram challenger. Show that only in the first run the
`publish` job runs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`publish` can be a placeholder that prints what it would push (it needs
credentials on GitHub). The evaluation set must be fixed — by seed here, by a
pinned file with a hash in practice — or the gate's decision would change from
run to run.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ob.write("gate.py", f'''
    """Block a challenger that is significantly worse than the champion (McNemar, one-sided)."""
    import sys

    import joblib
    import numpy as np
    from scipy.stats import binom

    sys.path.insert(0, {str(Path.cwd())!r})          # opsbook: the fixed evaluation set
    import opsbook as ob  # noqa: E402

    ALPHA = 0.05
    evaluation = ob.make_posts(4000, seed=300)
    y = evaluation.label.to_numpy()
    champion, challenger = joblib.load("model.joblib"), joblib.load("challenger.joblib")
    right_old = champion.predict(evaluation.text) == y
    right_new = challenger.predict(evaluation.text) == y
    b, c = int(np.sum(right_new & ~right_old)), int(np.sum(right_old & ~right_new))
    p = binom.sf(c - 1, b + c, 0.5) if b + c else 1.0
    print(f"champion {{right_old.mean():.4f}}, challenger {{right_new.mean():.4f}}")
    print(f"b = {{b}}, c = {{c}}, one-sided p = {{p:.3g}}")
    sys.exit(1 if p < ALPHA else 0)
''', base=repo)
wf = (repo / ".github/workflows/ci.yml").read_text()
wf += """
  gate:
    needs: image
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - name: Challenger vs champion
        run: python gate.py

  publish:
    needs: gate
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "would push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/sentiment:${{ github.sha }}"
"""
(repo / ".github/workflows/ci.yml").write_text(wf)
ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format -q . && {PY} -m ruff check -q --fix .", cwd=repo)   # keep the quality job green
ob.sh(f"{ob.tool('actionlint')} -no-color && echo 'actionlint: no problems'", cwd=repo, shown="actionlint")
challengers = {"retrained on a new sample": candidates["retrained on a new sample"],
               "unigrams only": candidates["unigrams only"]}
def gate_summary(text):
    return "\n".join(l for l in act_summary(text).splitlines()
                     if "gate" in l or "publish" in l or "champion" in l or "would push" in l
                     or "Failure" in l)
for name, ch in challengers.items():
    joblib.dump(ch, repo / "challenger.joblib")
    ob.run(f"git add -A && git commit -qm 'Challenger: {name}'", cwd=repo, env=GITENV, check=True)
    print(f"\n**Challenger: {name}**\n")
    ob.sh(act(repo), cwd=repo, shown="act push -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted", filt=gate_summary, timeout=1800)
```
With the retrained challenger the gate passes and `publish` runs; with the
unigram challenger `gate.py` exits with status 1, the job fails, and
`publish` — which `needs` it — never starts. The decision is reproducible
because the evaluation set is fixed; its power to detect a given degradation
can be planned as in @exr-ops6-cd-medium. A gate that only compares two
accuracy numbers would block good challengers by chance and pass bad ones on
small evaluation sets.
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The project's pipeline runs tests and style checks on
every push, builds the image, and — in a separate CD part — publishes it.
Follow this chapter: a `quality` job (format check, lint, tests, in the
fail-fast order) and an `image` job with a smoke test of meaning, linked by
`needs`; least-privilege `permissions`; a CD job restricted to the main branch
whose credentials come only from secrets; images tagged by commit. Validate
the workflow with actionlint before pushing. If the deployment to Hugging Face
Spaces is not done, describe it as in @sec-ops-cd (Docker Space,
`app_port`, token secret). When the pipeline retrains a model, gate its
promotion with a paired test on a fixed evaluation set (@exr-ops6-cd-hard).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Long-lived branches** and integration once a week: not CI, whatever the
  tooling.
- **Expensive stages first**, or everything sequential when it could run in
  parallel.
- **`continue-on-error`** on checks that should block.
- **Secrets in workflow files** or echoed in logs; `permissions` left at the
  default write access.
- **Unpinned actions** (`@main`): pin at least the major version, ideally the
  commit.
- **Rebuilding the image in CD** instead of promoting the one CI tested.
- **Model gates on two accuracy numbers**: use a paired test on a fixed set.
:::

## Summary

- CI integrates small changes often, each verified automatically; continuous
  delivery keeps every passing change releasable; continuous deployment
  releases it; continuous training retrains on new data. Delivery
  performance: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to
  restore.
- Sequential stages in increasing $c_i/p_i$ minimise the expected cost;
  parallel jobs finish at the weight of the critical path.
- GitHub Actions: workflows of jobs of steps; triggers, `needs`, matrices,
  caches keyed by lock-file hashes, least-privilege permissions, secrets,
  environments. actionlint checks workflows; act runs them locally.
- CD: separate jobs, main branch only, images tagged by commit, credentials
  from secrets; Hugging Face Docker Spaces as a deployment target.
- Model gates: McNemar's test uses only the disagreements, $c \sim
  \mathrm{Binomial}(b + c, \frac12)$ under equal accuracy, and is far more
  powerful than comparing two accuracies.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ops6-noninferiority}
**Non-inferiority.** A gate that blocks only *significantly* worse
challengers lets through any challenger tested on too few examples. Write a
**non-inferiority** gate instead: promote only if the data show, at the 5 %
level, that the challenger is *not worse by more than 1 point* — using the
normal approximation to the paired difference $(b - c)/n$, with variance
estimated by $(b + c)/n^2 - ((b - c)/n)^2/n$. Apply it to the two challengers
above with evaluation sets of 1 000 and 4 000 posts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def noninferior(y, p_old, p_new, margin=0.01, alpha=0.05):
    n = len(y)
    b = np.sum((p_new == y) & (p_old != y)); c = np.sum((p_old == y) & (p_new != y))
    diff = (b - c) / n
    var = (b + c) / n**2 - diff**2 / n
    lower = diff - norm.ppf(1 - alpha) * np.sqrt(var)
    return diff, lower, lower > -margin

for n in (1000, 4000):
    ev = ob.make_posts(n, seed=301)
    y = ev.label.to_numpy(); p_old = champion.predict(ev.text)
    for name, ch in candidates.items():
        d, lo, ok = noninferior(y, p_old, ch.predict(ev.text))
        print(f"n = {n}: {name:26s} difference {d:+.4f}, lower bound {lo:+.4f} -> {'promote' if ok else 'hold'}")
```
The burden of proof is now on the challenger: with 1 000 posts the evidence
may not suffice even for a good challenger (it is *held*, not promoted),
whereas the "not significantly worse" gate would have let it through by
default. With 4 000 posts the good challenger is shown non-inferior and the
unigram model is held. Choosing between the two gates is a policy decision:
non-inferiority is the safer default for automatic promotion.
:::

::: {#exr-ops6-dora}
**Delivery metrics from a log.** From a list of deployments with their commit
times, deployment times and whether they caused an incident (and when it was
resolved), compute the four delivery metrics. Write the function and apply it
to a small invented log; say which number you would try to improve first if
lead time were three days and the change failure rate 30 %.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from datetime import datetime as dt, timedelta as td
log = [  # (commit time, deploy time, incident resolved after, or None)
    (dt(2026, 11, 2, 9), dt(2026, 11, 5, 10), None), (dt(2026, 11, 3, 15), dt(2026, 11, 6, 11), td(hours=5)),
    (dt(2026, 11, 9, 10), dt(2026, 11, 12, 9), None), (dt(2026, 11, 10, 8), dt(2026, 11, 13, 16), td(hours=20)),
    (dt(2026, 11, 16, 11), dt(2026, 11, 19, 10), None), (dt(2026, 11, 17, 9), dt(2026, 11, 20, 15), td(hours=2)),
    (dt(2026, 11, 23, 14), dt(2026, 11, 26, 9), None), (dt(2026, 11, 24, 10), dt(2026, 11, 27, 12), None),
    (dt(2026, 11, 30, 9), dt(2026, 12, 3, 10), None), (dt(2026, 12, 1, 16), dt(2026, 12, 4, 9), None),
]
days = (max(d for _, d, _ in log) - min(d for _, d, _ in log)).days
lead = [d - c for c, d, _ in log]
failures = [r for _, _, r in log if r is not None]
print(f"deployment frequency {len(log) / days * 7:.1f} per week; median lead time "
      f"{sorted(lead)[len(lead) // 2]}; change failure rate {len(failures) / len(log):.0%}; "
      f"median time to restore {sorted(failures)[len(failures) // 2]}")
```
Lead times of three days with a 30 % failure rate point at large, infrequent
batches: the first lever is usually to make changes smaller and the pipeline
faster (CI on every change, automated tests and gates), which tends to lower
the failure rate too — the observation behind @forsgren2018's finding that
speed and stability improve together.
:::

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @fowler2006 — the original description of continuous integration and its
  practices; @humble2010, ch. 1–5 — the deployment pipeline.
- @forsgren2018, ch. 1–2 — measuring delivery performance; the four metrics.
- @githubactions2026 — workflow syntax (`on`, `jobs`, `needs`, `strategy`,
  `permissions`, `concurrency`), contexts and expressions, caching, secrets
  and environments; @actionlint2026 and @act2026 for checking and running
  workflows locally.
- @mcnemar1947 — the test for paired proportions; @dietterich1998 — why
  McNemar's test is recommended for comparing two classifiers on one test set.
- @garey1973 — optimal sequencing of tests, of which the $c/p$ rule is the
  simplest case.
